Volume 14 · Chapter 02

Stochastic growth and real business cycles

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c01

By the endSolve a stochastic growth model and evaluate its empirical mechanisms.

Volume 14 · Chapter 2

Stochastic growth and real business cycles

After a technology improvement, an economy can consume more, install more capital, change hours, or combine all three. The direction of output is easy to guess; the division between these margins is an equilibrium question. An exactly solved economy below has no hours response at all. A nearby model with durable capital has a positive local response. Neither statement identifies the cause of an observed recession.

Capability. Specify and solve a stochastic growth economy; prove the scope of its optimality and competitive decentralization; construct and audit a local perturbation; and distinguish calibrated inputs, solved allocations, model moments and causal evidence. Five original worked cases and twelve solved exercises cover calculation, proof and research critique.

Prerequisites. Dynamic optimization and recursive methods supplies recursive state sufficiency, conditional Euler equations and shadow-value terminal arguments. Volumes 2–3 supply concavity, conditional expectation and covariance; Time-series econometrics supplies the distinction between a stochastic law and an identified shock. This chapter proves its unbounded-return verification explicitly. It does not apply a bounded sup-norm contraction theorem to log utility.

All numerical economies, moment targets, innovations and exercises here are synthetic instructional constructions. No historical dataset is downloaded or replicated. A period has no assigned calendar length unless stated; the full-depreciation benchmark is a proof and computation laboratory, not a quarterly calibration.

1. Primitives, information and equilibrium objects

There is a unit mass of identical households, one consumption/investment good, no population growth and no trend. At date t, inherited capital kt is predetermined and productivity zt>0 is observed. A finite set Z has transition matrix P: Pij≥0 and each row sums to one. Its law is exogenous to household choices and known. A history is (z0,…,zt); decisions may depend on that history but not tomorrow’s innovation. Labor nt∈[0,1] is hours per available unit of time, leisure is 1−nt, output and consumption are goods per household per period, and capital is a goods stock. Parameters satisfy 0<α,β<1, χ>0, 0<δ≤1. Technology and preferences are

yt=ztktαnt1−α,   ct+kt+1≤yt+(1−δ)kt,   E0∑t≥0βt[log ct+χ log(1−nt)].

Capital and consumption are nonnegative; positive consumption and n<1 are needed for finite utility. Set log 0=−∞. Initial capital k0>0 and initial productivity are given. Investment is it=kt+1−(1−δ)kt; our baseline restricts only kt+1≥0, allowing negative net investment down to sale of undepreciated capital. Adding i≥0 changes the feasible set and can bind. There is no government, trade, utilization choice, adjustment cost or idiosyncratic risk.

The planner internalizes technology and chooses a feasible adapted allocation. If V is the actual value, its formal recursion is

V(k,z)=sup0≤n≤1, 0≤k′≤zkαn1−α+(1−δ)k{log[zkαn1−α+(1−δ)k−k′]+χ log(1−n)+β∑z′P(z,z′)V(k′,z′)}.

The state (k,z) is sufficient because preferences are time separable and P has no additional history dependence. A process with news about future productivity would require that news in the state. A competitive household instead takes the aggregate capital path and prices as given and carries its own assets a. Its recursive state is (a,k,z); replacing a with k before taking an individual derivative incorrectly makes the household internalize aggregate prices.

Interior necessary conditions. Let λt=1/ct, wt=(1−α)yt/nt, rt=αyt/kt, and Rt=rt+1−δ. At a differentiable, interior optimum, finite history-contingent perturbations give

λt=βEt[λt+1Rt+1],   χ/(1−nt)=λtwt.

To derive the first, reduce ct by ε, increase kt+1 by ε, and at every successor increase consumption by its extra output plus surviving capital, leaving subsequent capital fixed. The expected derivative is −λt+βEtλt+1Rt+1. An interior ε of either sign forces zero. At a lower bound k′=0 only ε≥0 is feasible, so λt≥βEtλt+1Rt+1 when the derivatives exist. A separate upper investment bound reverses that inequality. Labor variation changes output by w ε and leisure by −ε, giving the second equality; an hours cap instead requires a one-sided condition. Equality is neither an existence theorem nor a global numerical certificate.

2. An exact stochastic solution and a complete verification

For this section set δ=1, retain any finite positive Z and any stochastic P, and define s=αβ, q=1−s and

n*= (1−α)/[1−α+χq],   g(k,z)=s zkα(n*)1−α,   c*(k,z)=q zkα(n*)1−α.

Thus labor is constant, while both saving and consumption are state contingent. This zero labor response is a property of the joint log/full-depreciation specification. It is not a universal RBC prediction and not an assumption of fixed labor.

Derivation, including the value constants. Put B=α/(1−αβ), D=1/(1−αβ), and try V(k,z)=B log k+A(z). For fixed n and y=zkαn1−α, maximize log(y−k′)+βB log k′. Its second derivative is negative and the objective tends to −∞ at either endpoint, so k′=βB y/(1+βB)=s y is the unique maximum. The remaining labor terms are D(1−α)log n+χlog(1−n). Their derivative decreases through zero at n*, with −∞ at both endpoints, proving the labor formula. The coefficient of log k is αD=B. Set

H=log q+βB log s+D(1−α)log n*+χlog(1−n*),   A=H·1+D log z+βPA.

The vector series A=∑j≥0βjPj(H·1+D log z) converges absolutely because P is a sup-norm nonexpansion and the finite vector is bounded. It solves the equation; two solutions differ by d=βPd, so ‖d‖∞≤β‖d‖∞ implies d=0. This is a contraction on the finite vector of constants, not a contraction on the unbounded function V over all positive capital. Substitution proves the candidate Bellman identity, but a tail argument is still required to identify its value with the infinite-horizon objective.

Feasibility and finite objective. Since s,q,n*,1−n*>0, the candidate stays strictly feasible from any k0>0. Let xt=log kt. Then xt+1=αxt+log s+(1−α)log n*+log zt. Bounded log z and α<1 imply |xt|≤|x0|+M/(1−α) for a finite M. Candidate log c is therefore bounded, its discounted expected utility is absolutely summable, and βT+1E V(kT+1,zT+1)→0. Iterating the Bellman equality gives J*=V.

Global optimality against every feasible adapted alternative. Feasible capital satisfies k′≤zmaxkα. Hence kt≤K=max{k0,zmax1/(1−α)}; consumption is also bounded above. The positive part of discounted utility is summable for every feasible alternative. Its objective is consequently a well-defined extended real number, possibly −∞. Alternatives with objective −∞ cannot beat the candidate.

Write Δ for alternative minus candidate. Concavity of log consumption, log leisure and Cobb–Douglas production gives, history by history,

u(c,n)−u(c*,n*)≤λ*Δc−χΔn/(1−n*)≤λ*[R*Δk−Δk′]+[λ*w*−χ/(1−n*)]Δn=λ*[R*Δk−Δk′].

The middle inequality uses alternative resource feasibility and the supporting tangent to production at positive candidate k,n; with δ=1, R*=r*. The candidate satisfies its labor equality. It also satisfies its Euler equality: since k′=s y and c′=q y′, βλ′r′=βα/(qk′)=1/(qy)=λ in every successor, before taking expectations. Multiply the displayed bound by βt, sum through T and use adapted Δkt plus the conditional Euler equality to cancel all intermediate terms. Δk0=0, so

E∑t=0Tβt(ut−u*t)≤−βTE[λ*TΔkT+1]≤βTE[λ*Tk*T+1]=βTs/q→0.

The second inequality uses alternative nonnegative capital; no terminal restriction is imposed on the alternative’s log value. The established objective limits permit T→∞, proving optimality over all adapted feasible allocations, including non-Markov plans. Strict concavity of utility makes any different positive-probability (c,n) at a finite date strictly worse: retain its strictly positive tangent gap while passing to the same tail limit. Given initial capital, equality of c,n and no optimal disposal then fixes the capital path. This proves allocation uniqueness up to null histories. It proves existence in the stated exact domain by explicit construction, not existence for every RBC extension.

Worked case 1. State-contingent saving with invariant labor

Take 1/3 for α, 3/4 for β and 2 for χ. Then (s,q,n*)=(1/4,3/4,4/13). With deterministic z=1, k′=k gives k̄=n* s1/(1−α); (k̄,ȳ,c̄)=(1/26,2/13,3/26). The rental rate and wage are (r̄,w̄)=(4/3,1/3); βr̄=1 and χ/(1−n*)=w̄/c̄.

Now hold inherited k=k̄ and observe z=11/10. Output, consumption and next capital become (11/65,33/260,11/260). Hours remain 4/13. These are exact level results, not a first-order 10% approximation. If tomorrow z′=1, tomorrow output relative to ȳ is (11/10)1/3; if z′=11/10, it is (11/10)4/3. The state inherited tomorrow is the same in either branch; tomorrow’s observed shock changes the decision after it is revealed.

For a distinct persistent shock exercise let log z∈{−h,h}, h=1/50, with probability 4/5 of staying in the same state. P is [[4/5,1/5],[1/5,4/5]], Etlog z′=ρ log z with ρ=3/5. Here D=4/3 and B=4/9. Because log z is an eigenvector of P, A(z)=H/(1−β)+[D/(1−βρ)]log z. The coefficient on log z is 80/33. Changing persistence changes continuation welfare and future distributions, although it does not change this exact current saving share. Certainty equivalence of this particular share does not eliminate risk from welfare or from state-contingent capital.

3. Construct the competitive equilibrium, including ownership

At each aggregate history let firms rent K,N≥0 and maximize zKαN1−α−rK−wN. Set r=αy*/k* and w=(1−α)y*/n*. The concavity supporting inequality bounds every firm’s profit by its candidate profit, and constant returns gives r k*+w n*=y*, hence zero profit. A scale ray may maximize profit; market clearing picks aggregate k*,n*. Firm choice need not be unique for equilibrium allocation to be unique.

Each household owns its initial physical capital a0=k0 and an equal share of firms. At exogenous history-dependent prices it chooses an adapted plan with a′≥0 and

c+a′≤w n+(r+1−δ)a+π,   0≤n≤1,   π=0.

We construct a sequential-markets equilibrium using capital alone: identical households face only the common aggregate shock and identical endowments. This is sufficient to implement this allocation; it is not a claim that a capital asset completes markets for heterogeneous households. Goods clear as c*+i*=y*, labor as aggregate n=n*, capital services as a=k*, and firms’ aggregate profits equal the distributed dividends. Expectations use the true P and the actual aggregate law g.

Household optimality is a separate proof. For a price-taking deviation the budget is linear, so utility concavity and the candidate intratemporal equality give u−u*≤λ*[R*Δa−Δa′]. The same Euler cancellation as above bounds its truncated utility gain by βTλ*Ta*T+1≤βTs/q. Candidate k and z are bounded away from zero and infinity along histories from the given initial state, so candidate wages and gross returns have finite uniform upper bounds. A feasible deviator has at+1≤wmax+Rmaxat, bounding log-positive consumption by C(1+t). Its discounted positive utility part is summable, so the limiting comparison is legitimate. Nonnegative deviating assets deliver the terminal bound. Therefore candidate household choices are globally optimal at these prices. Together with firm optimality and clearing, this establishes a competitive equilibrium in the exact domain; invoking planner optimality alone would have omitted this decentralization argument.

Worked case 2. Who receives the extra output?

Use the 10% productivity event from case 1. The new wage is 11/30; the rental rate is 22/15. Labor income wn and capital income rk are (22/195,11/195), summing to output 11/65. Goods uses are consumption 33/260 plus gross investment 11/260. No extra dividend may be added after distributing both marginal products: that would count the same output twice.

The intratemporal condition can be written n=1−χc/w when c,w are treated as given and this value lies in [0,1]. Holding c=c̄ while increasing the wage to 11/30 gives n=53/143, above 4/13. But equilibrium consumption also rises 10%, keeping c/w unchanged and restoring n=4/13. The fixed-consumption derivative is a compensated local incentive calculation, not the equilibrium labor response. More precisely c fixes marginal utility of wealth under log utility; it is not the Hicks compensation experiment for an entire lifetime budget.

Competitive optimality here supports a conditional welfare conclusion: within these common-shock, identical-agent, undistorted primitives, no feasible allocation improves representative expected utility. It does not establish that observed unemployment is voluntary, that real recessions are efficient, or that eliminating a measured technology series is a feasible policy.

4. Durable capital and a local perturbation

Return to 0<δ<1. The exact saving fraction generally disappears. At a deterministic interior steady state z̄=1, Euler, production, resources and labor give

r̄=β−1−1+δ,   k̄/n̄=(α/r̄)1/(1−α),   ȳ=k̄αn̄1−α,   c̄=ȳ−δk̄,   χ=(1−α)ȳ(1−n̄)/(n̄c̄).

Since r̄>δ and α<1, c̄/k̄=r̄/α−δ>0. One may choose χ and solve n̄, or choose a target n̄ and infer χ. In the latter procedure, matching average hours is a calibration restriction, not a successful independent moment prediction.

For strictly positive variables define a hat as a log deviation from this deterministic steady state; at=log zt. Assume Etat+1=ρat, |ρ|<1. A finite two-state chain scaled by a small amplitude supplies such a bounded shock. Linearizing the interior equilibrium equations yields

ŷ=a+αk̂+(1−α)n̂;
c̄ ĉ+k̄ k̂′=ȳ ŷ+(1−δ)k̄ k̂;
ĉ+n̂/(1−n̄)=ŷ;
ĉ=Eĉ′−βr̄ E(ŷ′−k̂′).

For the labor equation, d log(1−n)=−n̄ n̂/(1−n̄); combining χc/(1−n)=w with ŵ=ŷ−n̂ gives the displayed coefficient. In the Euler equation the log variation of R is (r̄/R̄)(ŷ−k̂)=βr̄(ŷ−k̂). At first order a deterministic steady state eliminates products of innovations and policy deviations. This discards precautionary corrections of second or higher order; it does not say risk is economically irrelevant.

Solving the local system. Seek ĉ=p k̂+qaa and k̂′=K k̂+L a. Define m=ȳ/k̄, dn=α+n̄/(1−n̄), U=1−δ+mα[1+(1−α)/dn], V=m[1+(1−α)/dn] and W=c̄/k̄+m(1−α)/dn. Then n̂=[(α−p)k̂+(1−qa)a]/dn, K=U−Wp and L=V−Wqa. Write Yk=α+(1−α)(α−p)/dn, Ya=1+(1−α)(1−qa)/dn, and Hp=p−βr̄(Yk−1). Euler matching requires

p=Hp(U−Wp),   qa=[HpV−ρβr̄(1+(1−α)/dn)]/[1+HpW−ρ(1+βr̄(1−α)/dn)].

The first is a quadratic, not an invitation to accept any numerical root. A stable local branch requires |K|<1 as well as |ρ|<1, a nonzero denominator and satisfied equilibrium residuals. For the numerical case below the other root is unstable. This calculation solves the first-order system around a known steady state. It does not prove global existence, uniqueness or welfare accuracy of the nonlinear partial-depreciation economy. A nonlinear branch theorem would require additional hypotheses and a proof beyond merely finding these coefficients.

Worked case 3. Local hours increase, and the approximation has measurable errors

Choose (α,β,δ,n̄,ρ)=(0.36,0.96,0.10,1/3,0.80). These are illustrative per-period inputs, not an estimated national economy. The steady state is (k̄,ȳ,c̄,χ)=(1.4313493991,0.5632624950,0.4201275551,1.7160883281). Solving the quadratic and choosing its stable branch gives (p,qa,K,L)=(0.5309533186,0.5010268306,0.8357581865,0.3925826524).

A surprise a=0.01 at unchanged inherited capital has first-order log responses (ĉ,n̂,ŷ,k̂′)=(0.0050102683,0.0058020136,0.0137132887,0.0039258265). Higher current productivity raises labor’s marginal product and induces more work on this branch; durable capital permits consumption smoothing and investment accumulation. On an expected impulse path, aj=ρja0 and k̂j+1=Kk̂j+Laj. Innovations at future dates would require conditioning on their realizations.

To audit the reported coefficients, insert them into all four linear equations at independent state vectors (k̂,a), including nonzero capital. To audit level feasibility, exponentiate the approximate c,n,k′ and compute exact y=exp(a)kαn1−α and the resource residual eg=c+k′−y−(1−δ)k. Exponentiation ensures positive c,k′, but cannot ensure n<1 or exact resources. At k̂=0, a=0.01 the residual is -0.0000368784 goods. At a=0.005 it is -0.0000091921; the ratio is near four, consistent with a quadratic truncation error. This is a two-point diagnostic, not a uniform error theorem. A positive residual would mean the suggested allocation spends unavailable goods.

For a conditional Euler audit, choose the bounded two-state process a∈{−ε,ε} with stay probability (1+ρ)/2, evaluate approximate policies at both successors with the same k′, and report 1−βcE(R′/c′), together with labor and goods residuals. An expected-path substitution into the nonlinear Euler equation misses Jensen effects. Residuals, stability and feasibility are necessary diagnostics; without a proved error bound they do not certify a global optimum. Near n=1, a borrowing boundary or very low capital, a local interior approximation can fail qualitatively.

5. Exact theoretical moments and what they can identify

Worked case 4. A perfect output-volatility match that fails three other moments

Return to the exact case with α=1/3, β=3/4, χ=2 and symmetric a=log z∈{−h,h}, h=1/50, stay probability 4/5. Its stationary shock probabilities are (1/2,1/2), mean zero, variance v=h² and persistence ρ=3/5. These are theoretical population moments, not sample estimates or HP-filtered statistics. Define xt=log(kt/k̄), where k̄ is the deterministic z=1 steady state. Then

xt+1=αxt+at,   ŷt=αxt+at=xt+1,   ĉt=ît=ŷt,   n̂t=0.

These log equations are exact, not a perturbation. The stationary solution xt=∑j≥0αjat−1−j exists because |a|≤h and the series converges absolutely. Any two initial capital logs driven by the same shocks differ by αt times their initial difference, proving convergence for stationary-shock initialization and uniqueness among bounded stationary solutions. For an arbitrary initial productivity state, the two-state transition formula gives P(at=h)−1/2=ρt[P(a0=h)−1/2]. Every fixed-length recent shock block therefore converges in law to its stationary block. Truncate the series after J terms: its remaining absolute tail is at most hαJ/(1−α), uniformly in history. First send t→∞ for the finite block and vanishing initial-capital term, then J→∞; this proves convergence of the joint state to the stationary law from arbitrary initial k>0 and productivity. A two-sided stationary chain can be constructed from its consistent finite-history probabilities; the convergent series then defines x. Thus the following moment equations are justified rather than assumed.

Put C=Cov(xt,at) and X=Var xt. Conditional mean persistence gives C=ρ(αC+v), so C=ρv/(1−αρ). Squaring the recursion gives X=α²X+v+2αC. Hence X=v(1+αρ)/[(1−αρ)(1−α²)] and Var ŷ=X. Also Cov(ŷt,ŷt+1)=αX+ρ(v+αC). Numerically (v,C,X)=(0.0004,0.0003,0.000675); output log standard deviation is 0.0259807621 and first autocorrelation is 7/9.

The model implies (σc/σy,σi/σy,σn/σy)=(1,1,0) for log deviations, while consumption, investment and output correlations equal one. Correlation with hours is undefined because hours variance is zero; it is not zero correlation. Consider explicitly fictional target ratios (0.7,2.4,0.8). Their model-minus-target gaps are (0.3,-1.4,-0.8). Setting h to match output volatility exactly cannot repair these ratios, which are independent of h. This is a meaningful model rejection against those supplied targets, even though one selected moment fits perfectly.

Given α,ρ and a target output standard deviation σ, the fitted shock size is h=σ√[(1−αρ)(1−α²)/(1+αρ)]. That is a transparent calibration equation. If α and ρ are also free, one volatility alone leaves a continuum of parameter combinations. Report which moments selected parameters and which were reserved for evaluation. Sampling uncertainty, alternative transformations, measurement errors and parameter sensitivity belong in an empirical exercise; no standard errors can be inferred from this population calculation alone.

Worked case 5. A measured productivity residual need not be a technology shock

Suppose actual services are uk and output is y=A(uk)αn1−α. An investigator observing y,k,n but not utilization u computes b=log y−αlog k−(1−α)log n=log A+αlog u. Around baseline ū=4/5 and α=1/3, a deviation Δb=±1/50 is compatible with either Δlog A=±1/50 and fixed u, or fixed A and Δlog u=±3/50. The latter has utilization levels (0.7534116269,0.8494692372), both feasible if u≤1. Every residual movement in this example can come from utilization without any change in A.

This proves nonidentification from that accounting residual alone. It does not construct an alternative general equilibrium: doing that would also require utilization costs, household incentives, prices and a law for the driving shock. Conversely, solving the technology-only RBC economy does not establish that the data’s residual is its exogenous z. To discriminate, specify an independently measured utilization series and its errors, or a credible instrument/restriction separating technology from demand-induced service intensity; then test implications not mechanically built into the residual. Output and input measurement errors, changing markups and omitted effort create further possible wedges but are not numerically modeled here.

Primary-literature critique. Prescott’s 1986 article uses growth restrictions and a measured productivity process to compare model-generated fluctuations with US series. It explicitly discusses input measurement error and notes that the basic model underpredicts relative hours variability, motivating richer specifications. Its parameter discipline is valuable: independent restrictions can prevent arbitrary cycle-by-cycle fitting. But a growth share or a steady-state hours target is not an independent observation of an intertemporal labor elasticity, and a residual process needs a maintained measurement model. The distinction matters before interpreting a volatility match as evidence for technology causation. Prescott, Theory Ahead of Business Cycle Measurement, Quarterly Review 10(4), printed pages 9 and 14–16.

Summers’s contemporaneous response challenges the evidential basis for key parameters, particularly labor substitution, and the lack of independent corroboration for the technology shocks. A fair use of that critique is to require separate evidence for a mechanism’s elasticities and shocks, not to infer that a model with disputed premises has invalid algebra. Our exact case demonstrates the distinction sharply: its proof is complete within its domain, yet its hours and volatility restrictions can fail external targets. The historical debate supplies competing methodological arguments; it is not current evidence adjudicating every later RBC model. Summers, Some Skeptical Observations on Real Business Cycle Theory, Quarterly Review 10(4), printed pages 23–24.

A reproducible quantitative workflow. State frequency, timing, units and stationary transformation; list parameters and the independent evidence or target selecting each; solve and check feasibility, terminal behavior and equilibrium residuals; generate population moments or clearly seeded finite samples; apply the same transformation to model and data; report fitting versus evaluation moments, uncertainty and sensitivity; then state the identifying restrictions needed for a causal interpretation. Higher numerical accuracy cannot repair a false shock interpretation. A richer model may improve fit while weakening identification if many new parameters absorb the same moments.

6. Exercises

  1. Timing and a changed shock. In the exact economy, fix inherited k and current z but change P so high productivity becomes more persistent. Derive what changes in current c,k′,n and in A. Explain why a forecast of tomorrow’s shock cannot be substituted for today’s observed z. Then identify the state missing if a public signal predicts z two dates ahead beyond what current z predicts.
  2. A new exact calibration. Set α=1/2, β=4/5, χ=3 and δ=1. Derive s,n*, the z=1 steady k,y,c,r,w and the shadow terminal ratio k′/c. Show both Euler and intratemporal equalities.
  3. Unbounded value, valid proof. Prove that V=B log k+A(z) is not bounded on k>0. Explain exactly which finite-vector contraction remains valid. Reproduce the global verification terminal bound against an arbitrary feasible adapted alternative and state why no lower bound on that alternative’s log capital is required.
  4. Competitive accounting and labor. In case 1 replace the impact shock with z=4/5. At k̄ compute y,c,k′,w,r, labor income and capital income. Compare actual labor with the labor that would solve the intratemporal equation if consumption were held at its original steady value. State who owns capital and profits and why a separate positive dividend breaks clearing.
  5. Impose an hours cap. Return to case 1 but require 0≤n≤1/4. Derive the optimal policy for every k>0,z∈Z; show the labor derivative’s sign at the cap, the consumption/saving split, the adjusted steady capital and the valid one-sided optimality argument. Do not merely insert the cap into an unconstrained first-order equality.
  6. Two local roots. Using the partial-depreciation primitives of case 3, express Hp=Ap+B0 and derive the quadratic WAp²+(WB0+1−UA)p−UB0=0. Compute both p roots and the corresponding K values. Explain why a small polynomial residual does not select the economically relevant local branch.
  7. Reliability under finite shocks. Use the case-3 first-order policy at k̂=0 with shock states ±ε and stay probability 0.9. Evaluate exact goods, intratemporal log and normalized Euler residuals at current a=+ε for ε=0.01 and 0.005. Specify both successor states and their common inherited capital. Explain the limits of the observed error scaling and why exponentiation alone does not enforce the hours ceiling.
  8. Exact moment sensitivity. Hold α=1/3,h=1/50 but make shocks iid (stay probability 1/2). Derive C, X, output standard deviation and lag-one autocorrelation. Do the relative consumption, investment and hours volatilities change? Can h now be chosen to reproduce case 4’s output variance despite the different autocorrelation?
  9. Fitting is not identification. An analyst calibrates h to match fictional σy=0.02, holding α=1/3,ρ=3/5. Compute h. A second analyst uses α=1/3,ρ=0 and fits the same moment. Compute the second h and explain which additional moment distinguishes these two maintained models and which causal claim it still cannot identify.
  10. A deceptive solver report. A program returns k′=θy, c=(1−θ)y and labor n=(1−α)/[1−α+χ(1−θ)] in a full-depreciation economy. It reports exact goods and labor residuals for any θ∈(0,1). Derive the normalized Euler residual 1−βcE(r′/c′), and evaluate θ=1/5 at the case-1 parameters. Is feasibility plus two zero residuals a sufficient certificate? State which residual and tail evidence repairs the report.
  11. Measurement transfer. Suppose α=2/5, baseline utilization ū=3/4, and an observed log residual increases 0.04. Construct both a technology-only and a utilization-only explanation, check utilization feasibility, and explain why these accounting explanations do not themselves prove two competitive equilibria. Give a four-part research design that could separate the mechanisms.
  12. Referee the causal and welfare claim. A fictional paper says: “We chose shock variance and leisure weight to match output volatility and average hours. Our Euler errors are tiny. Hence technology shocks cause most recessions, and stabilization cannot improve welfare.” Write a structured critique identifying what is calibrated, what is solved, what remains unidentified, what computational evidence is missing, and what welfare assumptions need evidence. Propose one decisive out-of-fit model test and one permissible narrower conclusion. Use the rubric below.
Complete solutions and critique rubrics

1. Timing

The shares s=αβ and q and labor n* depend only on α,β,χ. Holding current k,z fixed leaves all three current choices unchanged. A changes to (I−βP)−1(H·1+D log z); its values and expected future allocations generally change. Current production uses realized z; replacing it by E z′ changes the current resource constraint. A public signal with extra predictive content must be carried in an enlarged state (k,z,signal), with its joint transition. Current choices can still have the same exact functional form in this special domain, but conditional continuation values and forecasting require the richer state; sufficiency is about the law, not just a policy coincidence.

2. New exact calibration

s=2/5,q=3/5 and n*=(1/2)/(1/2+9/5)=5/23. Since 1/(1−α)=2, k̄=n*s²=4/115; ȳ=k̄/s=2/23; c̄=qȳ=6/115. Thus (s,n*,k̄,ȳ,c̄,r̄,w̄,k′/c)=(2/5,5/23,4/115,2/23,6/115,5/4,1/5,2/3). βr̄=1. Intratemporally, 3/(18/23)=23/6 and w/c=(1/5)/(6/115)=23/6. At every stochastic successor βr′/c′=βα/(qk′)=1/c, so the Euler equality holds statewise; βTk′/c=(2/3)βT→0.

3. The correct terminal proof

B>0, so V tends to −∞ as k↓0 and +∞ as k↑∞ with z fixed. It is not an element of bounded continuous functions on all positive capital. The finite vector map A↦H·1+D log z+βPA has contraction modulus β and a convergent geometric series. For allocation comparison, concavity and candidate labor optimality yield Δu≤λ*(r*Δk−Δk′); adaptedness and conditional Euler cancel the discounted intermediate terms. Nonnegative alternative terminal capital gives gain through T≤βTλ*Tk*T+1=βTs/q. Candidate log capital is bounded, making its objective finite; all feasible alternatives have bounded positive utility parts, so their objective limits exist in [−∞,finite]. Sending T→∞ proves the comparison. No evaluation of V at alternative terminal capital is used, so even arbitrarily negative alternative log capital does not invalidate this proof.

4. Lower productivity accounts

At z=4/5, (y,c,k′,w,r,wn,rk)=(8/65,6/65,2/65,4/15,16/15,16/195,8/195). Actual n=4/13. Fixed original c̄=3/26 would give n=1−2(3/26)/(4/15)=7/52, inside the interval but substantially lower. In equilibrium c and w both fall 20%, so their ratio and hours are unchanged. Households own physical capital and firms. Labor plus capital income equals output; zero firm profits imply zero dividends. Adding a positive dividend without a financing source gives household resources exceeding goods and violates ownership-consistent accounts.

5. Binding hours cap

After optimizing k′, the n-dependent objective is (8/9)log n+2log(1−n). Its derivative at n=1/4 is (8/9)/(1/4)−2/(3/4)=8/9>0. Its second derivative is negative, and its unconstrained maximum 4/13 exceeds the cap. Therefore n=1/4 is the global constrained optimum. The capital split remains k′=y/4,c=3y/4. At z=1, k̄=n*s3/2=1/32. For the verification, λw−χ/(1−n)>0 at the candidate cap; every feasible Δn≤0, so the omitted labor term is nonpositive. The same Euler cancellation and βTs/q tail prove global optimality. An equality at the cap would be false. The finite-vector value constants change through n, but the coefficient B is unchanged.

6. The stable and unstable roots

Expand Yk=α+(1−α)α/dn−(1−α)p/dn. Thus A=1+βr̄(1−α)/dn and B0=βr̄[1−α−(1−α)α/dn]. Substitution p=(Ap+B0)(U−Wp) gives the stated quadratic by collecting powers. Its roots are (-0.1693134596,0.5309533186); their K values are (1.2463732734,0.8357581865). Both satisfy the algebraic equation. The negative p root propagates a capital perturbation explosively and fails the desired stable local saddle-path selection. A residual tests an equation, not the terminal or stability selection. Even the stable root is a local linear solution, not a global nonlinear existence theorem.

7. Finite-shock audits

For each ε set current (k̂,a)=(0,ε), ĉ=qaε, n̂=(1−qa)ε/dn and k̂′=Lε. Exponentiate relative to the steady levels. Tomorrow’s states are (Lε,+ε) with probability 0.9 and (Lε,−ε) with probability 0.1; capital is identical across these branches because it was chosen before tomorrow’s shock. For each branch evaluate c′,n′ from the same policy and r′=αy′/k′. The intratemporal log residual is en=log[χc/((1−n)w)]. The normalized Euler residual is eE=1−βc[0.9R′+/c′++0.1R′−/c′−].

At ε=0.01, (eg,en,eE)=(-0.0000368784,0.0000126728,-0.0000094971). At ε=0.005 the tuple is (-0.0000091921,0.0000031621,-0.0000023721). Values use the unrounded policy solution. The approximate fourfold reduction is consistent with second-order errors around zero; it supplies neither a uniform bound nor a welfare-loss estimate. Large positive n̂ can give n̄ exp(n̂)≥1, despite positive consumption and capital; such a point must be rejected before evaluating log leisure. Resource residuals require reporting or a disclosed feasibility correction, and correcting consumption changes the other residuals.

8. Iid shocks

ρ=0 gives C=0, X=v/(1−α²)=0.00045. σy=0.0212132034 and the lag-one autocorrelation is α=1/3, since the new shock is independent of current output. The volatility ratios remain (1,1,0). To reproduce X=0.000675 use h=√[0.000675(1−1/9)]=0.0244948974. This matches variance while retaining autocorrelation 1/3 rather than 7/9.

9. One fitted moment

For ρ=3/5, h=0.02√(16/27)=0.0153960072. For ρ=0, h=0.02√(8/9)=0.0188561808. Both give σy=0.02 by construction. Output’s lag-one autocorrelation differs, 7/9 versus 1/3, so that reserved moment distinguishes these maintained models in population. A finite sample needs uncertainty assessment. Matching both moments would still not identify the residual as exogenous technology, exclude utilization or demand mechanisms, or establish a policy-invariant shock law.

10. Feasible but nonoptimal

With the same constant θ and labor in every period, c′=(1−θ)y′, r′=αy′/k′, so βcE(r′/c′)=βα y/k′=αβ/θ. The normalized Euler residual is 1−αβ/θ. For θ=1/5 and αβ=1/4 it equals -1/4. Goods clear identically and the chosen labor solves its intratemporal equality, but extra saving has a positive utility derivative: βEλ′r′−λ>0. One must check the intertemporal condition, all relevant inequality conditions, feasible histories and terminal behavior. θ=αβ restores the exact policy; k′/c=θ/(1−θ) is bounded and discounted tails vanish. A coarse-grid Euler residual alone, however small, would not replace the global verification proof.

11. Measurement transfer

Technology-only: raise log A by 0.04 and keep u=0.75. Utilization-only: hold A fixed and raise log u by 0.04/(2/5)=0.1, giving u=0.8288781886<1. Either yields the same residual change for the supplied measured k,n. Neither construction specifies optimal utilization, costs, market clearing or an invariant driving process, so it is not a full second equilibrium model.

A complete answer earns one point for each of four elements: an independent utilization/effort measure with units and error model; an explicit technology-versus-utilization mechanism including costs and timing; an identifying source of variation or justified restrictions, with threats and falsification tests; and a held-out implication plus uncertainty assessment using the same transformations. For example, measured machine operating hours could test the fixed-utilization restriction, but an error-prone proxy alone cannot guarantee identification.

12. Referee benchmark and ten-point rubric

Contribution and calibration (2 points). The paper may offer an internally disciplined stochastic economy, but volatility and average hours were used to choose shock variance and leisure weight. They cannot simultaneously be advertised as independent validation moments. Report parameter sources and sensitivity rather than calling every chosen input estimated.

Solution evidence (2 points). Tiny Euler residuals do not establish feasibility, household/firm optimality, market clearing, boundary conditions, stability or a terminal bound. Require these checks on the declared domain, clarify the numerical approximation and distinguish an exact theorem from a finite numerical audit.

Identification (2 points). A residual may include utilization, effort, markups or measurement errors. Specify an independent shock measure or valid restrictions and address competing mechanisms. A calibrated shock variance is not a causal estimate of the fraction of recessions due to technology.

Welfare (2 points). Planner equivalence is conditional on preferences, ownership, information, complete accounting and absence of relevant distortions. Actual interventions may change technology, risk, insurance or distortions; their feasible set and financing must be modeled. With heterogeneous households, distribution matters. An undistorted representative model cannot by itself establish the welfare ranking of real stabilization policies.

Falsifiable repair (2 points). Reserve the investment/consumption volatility ratio or hours-output comovement before fitting and assess it with uncertainty under common transformations. For the exact benchmark, any positive hours variance rejects its labor restriction against accurate measurements; no tuning of h repairs it. A defensible conclusion is: “Conditional on these primitives and the stated numerical domain, the computed model reproduces these selected moments; the mechanism and welfare claims require separate evidence.” Award credit for equally explicit tests and qualified conclusions, not for blanket approval or rejection of RBC research.

7. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In five minutes explain how a positive technology shock can raise wages without raising hours, why a planner solution needs an ownership-consistent decentralization, and why an excellent volatility fit need not identify a shock.

Benchmark answer. In the log/full-depreciation economy consumption and wages rise in the same proportion, leaving χc/w and labor unchanged; partial depreciation changes the intertemporal allocation and the local labor response can become positive. Firms must maximize at the quoted factor prices, households must optimize taking those prices as given, all profits must be assigned to owners and goods/factors must clear. One fitted volatility supplies one restriction; it neither validates other moment implications nor proves that a measured residual is technology rather than utilization or another omitted component.

Delayed retention, one week later without the chapter. (1) State the exact saving share and terminal ratio. (2) With β=3/4 and α=1/3, does a claimed policy θ=1/5 satisfy Euler? (3) Can the exact model produce positive hours variance by increasing shock size? (4) State one thing a stable local root does not prove.

Answer key. (1) s=αβ and k′/c=s/(1−s), with discounted ratio vanishing. (2) No: 1−αβ/θ=−1/4. (3) No: n is constant for every shock history under these primitives. (4) It does not prove global nonlinear existence, unique equilibrium, feasibility far from the expansion point, a uniform error bound or causal identification; any one correctly explained limitation suffices.

Next step. Incomplete markets and heterogeneous agents (planned successor) replaces identical wealth and aggregate-only risk with household distributions, borrowing constraints and precautionary choices. There the distribution can be a state, individual assets differ from aggregate capital, and the representative planner shortcut requires a new argument. The exact saving-share and constant-hours formulas proved here do not automatically survive.

Sources and further study

  • Edward C. Prescott, Theory Ahead of Business Cycle Measurement — Equilibrium household/firm/state/accounting structure and the historical calibration/productivity-measurement/hours-moment discussion.
  • Lawrence H. Summers, Some Skeptical Observations on Real Business Cycle Theory — Contemporaneous parameter-evidence and labor-substitution objections; opening challenge to independent technology-shock corroboration.
